tEn: Yann LeCun: Intelligence Is Adaptability, Not Memorized Text
tZh: Yann LeCun：智能是适应力，而非记忆文本
sEn: Yann LeCun argues that large language models merely memorize the internet rather than reason, and explains why true intelligence means adapting to new situations through world models.
sZh: Yann LeCun 认为大语言模型只是在记忆互联网而非推理，并阐释真正的智能在于通过世界模型快速适应新情境。

consensus.en: Intelligence is adaptability: quickly learning new skills and understanding new situations with minimal interaction.
consensus.zh: 智能即适应力：以最少交互快速学习新技能并理解新情境。

consensus.en: LLMs memorize and regurgitate; they lack true reasoning, planning, and creativity.
consensus.zh: 大语言模型只是记忆和复述，缺乏真正的推理、规划与创造力。

consensus.en: World models enable prediction and planning; they are essential for human-level intelligence.
consensus.zh: 世界模型支持预测与规划，是实现人类水平智能的关键。

consensus.en: JEPA learns abstract representations to predict only what is predictable, ignoring unpredictable details.
consensus.zh: JEPA学习抽象表征，只预测可预测部分，忽略不可预测细节。

consensus.en: Open foundation models are safer and more innovative than closed, proprietary systems.
consensus.zh: 开放基础模型比封闭专有系统更安全、更具创新性。

consensus.en: Regulate AI applications, not research and development; development-level regulation is obscurantism.
consensus.zh: 应监管AI应用而非研发；研发层面的监管是蒙昧主义。

contrarian.en: Scaling LLMs on text is a dead end for true intelligence; world models are the right path.
contrarian.zh: 文本大语言模型的Scaling是通向真正智能的死胡同，世界模型才是正途。

contrarian.en: AI is not intrinsically dangerous; the danger narrative serves incumbents' interests.
contrarian.zh: AI并非内在危险；危险叙事服务于现有掌控者的利益。

contrarian.en: Open source AI is the best path to safety, contrary to claims by OpenAI and Anthropic.
contrarian.zh: 开源AI才是安全的最佳路径，与OpenAI和Anthropic的主张相反。

contrarian.en: Superintelligence will amplify humans and do our bidding, not take over.
contrarian.zh: 超级智能将增强人类并服从我们，而非接管世界。

contrarian.en: Current LLMs are intrinsically unsafe because they are not objective-driven and lack world models.
contrarian.zh: 当前大语言模型因非目标驱动且缺乏世界模型，本质不安全。

contrarian.en: AI bioweapon and takeover fears are overblown; biologists laugh at the scenario.
contrarian.zh: AI生物武器和接管世界的恐惧被夸大；生物学家对此嗤之以鼻。

turns.en: Hi and welcome to Futurology. I'm your host, Dawn Nakagawa, and in this episode we have an interview between myself and Yann LeCun. Yann LeCun is the founder and chairman of AMI Labs, a Paris startup, and he's the winner of the Turing Award, which he won along with Geoffrey Hinton and Joshua Bengio in 2018. Yann started his career back in the '80s at Bell Labs, where he was teaching computers to see. He went on to work at Facebook and to build their AI lab, but eventually left in 2025. Yann sees things quite differently than most of the field of AI right now. His contention, and it's quite convincing, is that the human brain doesn't develop on language. Most of what the brain learns is through its contextual awareness and its senses. So he's building a world model, a model that will be able to predict what happens next, not just what word comes next. As a result, Yann doesn't believe the hype around the dangers of the current model, and he believes that we're being told that because it serves the interests of those that currently control this technology. So with that, let's go to the interview with myself and Yann on Futurology.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听《未来学》。我是主持人 Dawn Nakagawa，本期节目是我对 Yann LeCun 的访谈。Yann LeCun 是巴黎初创公司 AMI Labs 的创始人兼董事长，也是图灵奖得主，2018 年他与 Geoffrey Hinton、Joshua Bengio 共同获奖。Yann 在 80 年代于贝尔实验室开启职业生涯，在那里教计算机“看”。之后他去了 Facebook，搭建了他们的 AI 实验室，但最终在 2025 年离开。Yann 对当前 AI 领域的看法与大多数人相当不同。他的观点——而且相当有说服力——是人脑并非基于语言发展。大脑学到的大部分东西都来自情境感知和感官。所以他正在构建一个世界模型，一个能预测接下来会发生什么、而不只是预测下一个词是什么的模型。因此，Yann 不相信当前围绕模型危险的炒作，他认为有人这样告诉我们，是因为这符合那些目前掌控这项技术的人的利益。那么，让我们进入我对 Yann 的访谈。

turns.en: Yann LeCun, welcome to Futurology.
turns.zh: Yann LeCun，欢迎来到《未来学》。

turns.en: Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请。

turns.en: I thought we could start at the beginning, so to speak. You have pretty strong views about the approach to creating intelligence and how humans do it and how frontier models are best trained. What is your view on intelligence? Like what's your definition of it? How do we develop it?
turns.zh: 我想我们可以从头说起。你对创造智能的路径、人类如何做到这一点，以及如何最好地训练前沿模型，都有相当鲜明的观点。你对智能的看法是什么？比如你的定义是什么？我们如何发展它？

turns.en: There's many definitions, but we know what it's not. It's not a collection of declarative knowledge. It's not a collection of skills. My definition would be it's an ability to apprehend new situations and learn new skills extremely quickly with minimal interaction in the world. It's human intelligence that allows any teenager to learn to drive in 20 hours of practice.
turns.zh: 定义有很多，但我们知道它不是什么。它不是一堆陈述性知识，也不是一堆技能。我的定义是：它是一种领会新情境、并以极少与世界的交互极快地学习新技能的能力。正是人类智能让任何一个青少年只需 20 小时的练习就能学会开车。

turns.en: We have literally billions of hours of training data of people driving cars around, and we still can't use that to get a machine to learn to drive as reliably as humans. So this sort of adaptability and ability to apprehend new situations, clearly. There's a quote — it's not really a quote, it's an apocryphal quote from Jean Piaget, the developmental psychologist, who didn't say it but could have said: intelligence is not what you know, it's what you do when you don't know.
turns.zh: 我们有字面意义上数十亿小时的人开车训练数据，却仍然无法用它让机器像人一样可靠地学会开车。所以就是这种适应性，以及领会新情境的能力，很明显。有一句话——其实不算原话，是发展心理学家 Jean Piaget 的一句伪托名言，他没说过但完全可能说：智能不在于你知道什么，而在于你不知道时怎么做。

turns.en: So you're facing a new situation but you have enough background knowledge about how the world works to figure out what to do without necessarily having seen someone else in the same situation or without having trained yourself to do that.
turns.zh: 也就是说，你面对一个新情境，但你对世界如何运作有足够的背景知识，从而能想出该怎么做，而不必见过别人处于同样情境，也不必事先专门训练过。

turns.en: So your idea of developing intelligence and the way to go about it would be closer to training a car on a road than it would be to training an LLM on all the volume of human knowledge, written knowledge.
turns.zh: 所以你对发展智能的思路，更接近于在道路上训练一辆车，而不是用海量人类知识、书面知识去训练一个大语言模型。

turns.en: So when you train an LLM on human-produced knowledge from text but also artificial data, you're training that system to accumulate previously known knowledge, declarative knowledge. That's not intelligence, that's memory. It's rote learning. It's not reasoning, it's not invention, it's not creativity, it's not adaptivity.
turns.zh: 当你用文本中人类生产的知识、也包括人工数据来训练一个大语言模型时，你是在训练那个系统去积累已知的知识、陈述性知识。那不是智能，那是记忆。那是死记硬背。它不是推理，不是发明，不是创造力，也不是适应性。

turns.en: And so it's not really the kind of intelligence that we observe in animals. And also the type of techniques that are used by LLMs only work when you train them on sequences of discrete symbols. They don't really handle natural signals very well.
turns.zh: 所以它并不是我们在动物身上观察到的那种智能。而且大语言模型所用的那类技术，只有在用离散符号序列训练时才有效。它们并不能很好地处理自然信号。

turns.en: So an LLM is trained to basically predict the next word in the text, right? You train it on a big sequence of words or symbols, whatever they are, and it's trying to predict the next symbol in the sequence. When you try to apply this to natural signals like say video or audio, it doesn't really work. And the reason is that most of the information in a natural signal like video is completely unpredictable.
turns.zh: 大语言模型基本上就是被训练来预测文本中的下一个词，对吧？你用一大串词或符号——不管是什么——来训练它，它试图预测序列中的下一个符号。当你试图把这套方法用到视频或音频这样的自然信号上时，它并不奏效。原因是，像视频这样的自然信号中，大部分信息是完全不可预测的。

turns.en: And so you train a system to do something it can't do, and it doesn't really work. So you have to use other approaches for that.
turns.zh: 所以你是在训练一个系统去做它做不到的事，那自然行不通。所以你必须为此采用其他方法。

turns.en: But is it truly unpredictable? I mean, you think about — let's say you were training it on images of trees, I'm just saying, right? It at some point should recognize that as you go vertically up a tree, at some point you're going to hit something that's green and has leaves and so on. So there is a certain amount — if you look at the visual space, it's not purely predictive, but you can, just like the way humans do, kind of intuit what it is that's going to be present in a specific kind of landscape or a kind of view.
turns.zh: 但它真的不可预测吗？我是说，你想想——假设你用树的图像来训练它，我只是举个例子，对吧？它到某个时候应该能认识到，当你沿着一棵树往上走，某个时候你会碰到绿色的、有叶子的东西等等。所以存在一定的——如果你看视觉空间，它并非纯粹可预测，但你可以像人类那样，凭直觉知道在某种特定的景观或视野中会出现什么。

turns.en: You're absolutely right. But the issue is you cannot predict it in all details. So if you look at the trunk of a tree and you slowly move your eyes up, you can certainly predict at some point there's going to be leaves and things like that, you know, unless it's that time of the year when it is—
turns.zh: 你说得完全对。但问题在于你无法预测所有细节。所以如果你看着树干，慢慢把视线往上移，你当然能预测某个时候会出现叶子之类的东西，除非正好是那个季节——

turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: But even that you can predict. There's no way you can predict the shape and position of every leaf, right? Whereas if you train a system to predict what's going to happen in that video — you show the initial segment of the video of the camera moving up the tree and you ask the system to predict what's going to happen next — there's no way it can predict this at the pixel level. It cannot predict all the details. And it's certainly not going to predict the random motion of the leaves due to the wind, or whether some particular bird is sitting on a branch, right?
turns.zh: 但即便是那个你也能预测。可你没法预测每一片叶子的形状和位置，对吧？而如果你训练一个系统去预测那段视频里接下来会发生什么——你给它看摄像机沿树往上移动的视频开头一段，让它预测接下来会发生什么——它绝无可能在像素层面预测出来。它无法预测所有细节。它当然也预测不了叶子被风吹动的随机运动，或者某只特定的鸟是否停在树枝上，对吧？

turns.en: So that's what I'm saying: there's a part of the information that is predictable, but most of the information isn't. And so the techniques that are used to predict words in a text do not work.
turns.zh: 所以这就是我说的：有一部分信息是可预测的，但大部分信息不是。因此，用于预测文本中词语的那类技术行不通。

turns.en: You can never predict exactly which word follows the text, but there's only a finite number of words in the dictionary, and you can produce a probability distribution over every word in your dictionary. And that's how LLMs work really. They produce a score for every word. Then they pick a high-scoring word from that prediction and shift it into the input, and then predict the second word, shift that into their input, and then the third word. That's called autoregressive prediction. A very old concept.
turns.zh: 你永远无法精确预测文本后面跟着哪个词，但词典里的词是有限的，你可以对词典中每个词生成一个概率分布。大语言模型实际上就是这么工作的。它们为每个词打一个分，然后从预测中挑一个高分词，把它移入输入，再预测第二个词，再移入输入，然后是第三个词。这叫做自回归预测。一个非常古老的概念。

turns.en: If you try to apply the same kind of concept to video, trying to predict what's going to happen in the video at the pixel level, it simply doesn't work.
turns.zh: 如果你尝试将同样的概念应用到视频上，试图在像素级别预测视频中会发生什么，那根本行不通。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I've been working on this for like the better part of the last 20 years and mostly failing for the first because I was trying to predict at the pixel level. The solution to this, or my solution to this, which we're still working on, is what we call JEPA. So that means joint embedding predictive architecture. It's basically a way for a system to learn an abstract representation of the input which eliminates a lot of details that are unpredictable and only preserve the part that is predictable. So the system simultaneously learns a representation of the input that allows it to make prediction and trains itself to predict. And eliminates all the details that are not predictable like the individual position and size of the leaves or the branches on the tree. But the representation is rich enough to tell you there's going to be branches and leaves.
turns.zh: 我研究这个已经差不多 20 年了，最初大部分都失败了，因为我试图在像素级别进行预测。这个问题的解决方案，或者说我的解决方案，我们仍在研究中，就是我们所说的 JEPA。意思是联合嵌入预测架构。它基本上是一种让系统学习输入的抽象表示的方法，这种表示消除了许多不可预测的细节，只保留可预测的部分。所以系统同时学习输入的表示，使其能够进行预测，并训练自己进行预测。它消除了所有不可预测的细节，比如树叶或树枝的个别位置和大小。但表示足够丰富，可以告诉你会有树枝和树叶。

turns.en: Right. And so that abstract representation is still visual. It's still an image.
turns.zh: 对。所以那个抽象表示仍然是视觉的。它仍然是一张图像。

turns.en: It's abstract. It's something the neural net learns internally that you may train another neural net to try to decode like what is the thing thinking about? What is it predicting? And it may predict something that's kind of blurry a little bit because it doesn't have all the information about individual positions of the leaves.
turns.zh: 它是抽象的。它是神经网络内部学习到的东西，你可以训练另一个神经网络来尝试解码，比如这个东西在思考什么？它在预测什么？它可能会预测出有点模糊的东西，因为它没有关于树叶个别位置的所有信息。

turns.en: This is your approach to creating what you call a world model, correct? And so explain to me what a world model is.
turns.zh: 这是你创建所谓世界模型的方法，对吗？那么请向我解释一下什么是世界模型。

turns.en: So world model is what allows humans, animals, and artificial systems to predict the consequences of their actions and using those predictions to plan a sequence of actions to accomplish a task. So we do this all the time. Animals do this as well. If you have some idea of the state of the world at time T and you imagine taking an action, can you predict the state of the world at time T plus one after you've taken the action, done the intervention. There's also the ability to predict how the world is going to evolve even if you don't take any action. So if you have this kind of mental model of the world you can predict the consequences of taking a series of actions and if you have a particular goal in mind, an action you want to accomplish, you want to fill up a glass with water or something, you can predict if a particular sequence of actions will accomplish this task and therefore you can figure out a sequence of actions that will accomplish the task and that's planning.
turns.zh: 世界模型是让人类、动物和人工系统能够预测其行动后果，并利用这些预测来规划一系列行动以完成任务的东西。我们一直这样做。动物也是如此。如果你对时间 T 的世界状态有一些了解，并想象采取一个行动，你能预测在采取行动、进行干预之后，时间 T+1 的世界状态吗？还有能力预测世界将如何演变，即使你不采取任何行动。所以如果你有这种心理模型，你可以预测采取一系列行动的后果，如果你有特定的目标，一个你想完成的行动，你想把杯子装满水之类的，你可以预测某个行动序列是否能完成这个任务，因此你可以找出一个能完成任务的行动序列，那就是规划。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: It's very classical in engineering when you want to plan the trajectory of a robot arm or something like this, this is called motion planning or there's a whole subfield of engineering called optimal control where people do this kind of stuff but the models they use generally are models that are in the form of a few equations that are written by engineers and scientists that allow to predict the next state of a robot arm or a car or an airplane given a controls that you send it. What humans and animals do is they learn those models of the world by observation but also by interaction. So that's what allows me to tell that there's a glass on the small table here, if I push on the glass it's going to slide on the table, if I push on the table with the same force it's not going to move. We have all of those kind of intuitive notions about reality that we build and we learn when we are babies in the first few weeks and months of life. It takes human babies about nine months to learn about gravity for example to realize that every object will fall unless supported, with a few exceptions of objects that float in the air that actually get babies to stare at them.
turns.zh: 这在工程中非常经典，当你想规划机械臂的轨迹或类似的东西时，这被称为运动规划，或者有一个完整的工程子领域叫做最优控制，人们做这种事情，但他们使用的模型通常是由工程师和科学家编写的几个方程形式的模型，可以预测机械臂、汽车或飞机的下一个状态，给定你发送的控制指令。人类和动物所做的是通过观察，也通过互动来学习这些世界模型。所以这让我能够判断这里小桌子上有一个玻璃杯，如果我推玻璃杯，它会在桌子上滑动，如果我用同样的力推桌子，它不会移动。我们在婴儿时期的前几周和几个月里建立并学习了所有这些关于现实的直觉概念。例如，人类婴儿大约需要九个月来学习重力，意识到每个物体都会下落，除非有支撑，除了少数漂浮在空中的物体会让婴儿盯着看。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: So those things are not like we're not born with them. We learn them by observation. And that's the type of learning that I think we should reproduce in machines if we want them to understand the world.
turns.zh: 所以这些东西不是我们与生俱来的。我们通过观察学习它们。我认为如果我们想让机器理解世界，就应该在机器中复制这种学习方式。

turns.en: So how do you do that? How do you help them develop a world model?
turns.zh: 那么你如何做到这一点？你如何帮助它们发展世界模型？

turns.en: So let's say we want to do this like babies and baby animals. Initially just train a system to predict what's going to happen in a video. Take a big collection of videos, video clips. Show the first half to the system and ask it to predict what's going to happen next. But again using those architectures that learn an abstract representation of the input and train itself to predict at the representation level. Those JEPA joint embedding predictive architectures. So you show the video to the system. The system runs it to an encoder that produces this abstract representation and within this representation space trains itself to predict the future very much like an LLM is trying to predict the next word except that here you predict the next abstract representation of the observation from the world.
turns.zh: 假设我们想像婴儿和幼小动物那样做。最初只是训练一个系统来预测视频中会发生什么。取一个大的视频集合，视频片段。向系统展示前半部分，并要求它预测接下来会发生什么。但再次使用那些学习输入的抽象表示并训练自己在表示级别进行预测的架构。那些 JEPA 联合嵌入预测架构。所以你向系统展示视频。系统将其运行到一个编码器，产生这个抽象表示，并在这个表示空间内训练自己预测未来，非常像 LLM 试图预测下一个词，只不过这里你预测的是来自世界的观察的下一个抽象表示。

turns.en: So do you think it's possible to do that just on video? Like don't you think at some point it should be embodied in order to move around the world in some way?
turns.zh: 那么你认为仅靠视频就能做到吗？你不觉得在某个时候它应该被具身化，以便以某种方式在世界中移动吗？

turns.en: Right. So the process that I just described is not really an external world model on which you do not act. You just observe what the world is doing and predicting what's going to happen. But if you want a world model you can use for planning and actions then you need it to be action conditioned. So basically it would be an observation of like here is a short video of the state of the world and right now I'm sending these commands to a robot arm. And then here is the next segment of video where the robot arm has received those commands. And so now what you can train the system to do is state at time T, action, state at time T plus one. And you can see babies learning that model of themselves when they're babies, right? Like young babies just gesticulate, they kind of randomly move their limbs. They're basically building a dynamical model of their own limbs and their own body. And once in a while they will hit themselves.
turns.zh: 对。所以我刚才描述的过程并不是一个你不采取行动的外部世界模型。你只是观察世界在做什么并预测会发生什么。但如果你想要一个可以用于规划和行动的世界模型，那么你需要它是行动条件化的。所以基本上它会是这样的观察：这里是一段关于世界状态的短视频，现在我正在向机械臂发送这些命令。然后这里是下一段视频，机械臂已经收到了那些命令。所以现在你可以训练系统做的是：时间 T 的状态，动作，时间 T+1 的状态。你可以看到婴儿在婴儿时期学习自己的模型，对吧？就像小婴儿只是做手势，他们随机移动四肢。他们基本上在建立自己四肢和身体的动态模型。偶尔他们会打到自己。

turns.en: Babies start sucking their thumb without realizing it, and it's very haphazard at first. Then very quickly they realize they can deliberately move their thumb to their mouth. So that's a similar way a system can learn. Later, it takes about three or four months before babies can actually reach for an object and grab it, which is the same kind of learning.
turns.zh: 婴儿开始吸吮拇指时并没有意识到，一开始非常随意。但很快他们意识到自己可以有意识地移动拇指到嘴边。所以系统学习的方式也类似。之后，大约三四个月后，婴儿才能实际伸手抓物体，这是同一种学习。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: We're having those discussions with a colleague at NYU, Karen Adolph. She has a baby lab, so she has babies in her lab doing all kinds of stuff, and she studies how babies learn motor control. When I say that a lot of what we learn about the world is purely by observation, she says, 'You're crazy, that's completely false, we interact all the time.' So she disagrees with me.
turns.zh: 我们和纽约大学的同事凯伦·阿道夫有过这些讨论。她有一个婴儿实验室，实验室里有婴儿做各种事情，她研究婴儿如何学习运动控制。当我说我们关于世界的很多学习纯粹是通过观察时，她说：‘你疯了，那完全不对，我们一直在互动。’所以她不同意我的观点。

turns.en: It seems like it would make the most sense that to really develop a world model you need all of it, right?
turns.zh: 看起来最合理的是，要真正开发一个世界模型，你需要所有这些，对吧？

turns.en: At a certain level of abstraction, language is useful to describe what happens in the world. Humans learn a lot from language. And it is itself an abstraction, a representation. It's not a universal abstraction—there's a lot of very low-level stuff we have a hard time describing in language—but above a certain level of abstraction, language is really useful. So there's no question: if you want robots to do things similar to what humans do, at some point you're going to have to use language. And this is basically what a lot of current AI systems are doing. They're using language as an indispensable component.
turns.zh: 在一定的抽象层次上，语言对于描述世界上发生的事情很有用。人类从语言中学到很多。语言本身是一种抽象，一种表征。它不是通用的抽象——有很多非常低层次的东西我们很难用语言描述——但在一定抽象层次以上，语言确实非常有用。所以毫无疑问：如果你想让机器人做类似人类做的事情，在某个时刻你就必须使用语言。这基本上也是当前很多 AI 系统在做的事情。它们把语言作为不可或缺的组成部分。

turns.en: Right. But like how does a cat learn? You see a cat sitting at the bottom of a piece of furniture, moving its head. All of a sudden the cat goes bounce bounce bounce and it's on top of the furniture, and you haven't figured out how it could possibly do this by bouncing off the walls.
turns.zh: 对。但猫是怎么学习的？你看到一只猫坐在家具底部，晃着头。突然猫弹弹弹就上了家具顶部，你还没搞明白它怎么能通过弹墙做到这一点。

turns.en: Or it estimates how high it has to leap to get to the top of the bookshelf or something.
turns.zh: 或者它估计要跳多高才能到达书架顶部之类的。

turns.en: Bouncing on the wall and realizing there's enough grip there to bounce off.
turns.zh: 在墙上弹跳，并意识到那里有足够的抓地力可以弹开。

turns.en: It has its own world model. It has a very accurate model of its own dynamics, but also its interaction with the environment—whether it can have a grip on the wallpaper, what material it is, what friction, etc. They're not perfect; sometimes they make mistakes—you see those funny videos on YouTube—but it's amazing how good they are. And we cannot reproduce this with machines at the moment. Even though we can build robots that have good physical abilities, the smarts that go into modeling the world and the robot's interaction with the world is way below what cats can do.
turns.zh: 它有自己的世界模型。它对自己的动力学有非常准确的模型，还有与环境的互动——能否抓住墙纸、是什么材料、摩擦力如何等等。它们并不完美；有时会犯错——你在 YouTube 上看到那些搞笑视频——但它们的能力令人惊叹。而我们目前无法用机器复制这一点。即使我们能建造具有良好物理能力的机器人，但用于建模世界和机器人交互的智能远低于猫的能力。

turns.en: So at some point you have to bring them all together in order to even come close to—I don't know, you don't like the term AGI—but come close to human-level intelligence, correct?
turns.zh: 所以在某个时刻，你必须把它们全部整合起来，才能接近——我不知道，你不喜欢 AGI 这个词——但接近人类水平的智能，对吧？

turns.en: Well, yes, but I think we figured out the language part. And we figured that it's easy. That's how we got there first because it's discrete, because the issue of not being able to predict exactly which word follows the text can be dealt with by producing a probability distribution over words. And it doesn't work for natural signals of the real world. We do not have a good way of representing a probability distribution over every video segment. We just don't. It's a mathematically intractable problem. So it's not a question of our computers not being powerful enough. It's just impossible.
turns.zh: 嗯，是的，但我认为我们已经解决了语言部分。我们发现它很容易。这就是为什么我们先到达那里，因为它是离散的，因为无法准确预测文本中下一个词的问题可以通过生成词的概率分布来处理。但这不适用于现实世界的自然信号。我们没有好的方法来表示每个视频片段的概率分布。我们就是没有。这是一个数学上棘手的问题。所以这不是我们的计算机不够强大的问题。这根本不可能。

turns.en: So Fei-Fei Li, who is also on the Futureology podcast, is doing something similar to you, correct? She's No? Okay. So because my understanding is she was training models on video, but okay. So explain to me the difference.
turns.zh: 所以李飞飞，她也上过 Futureology 播客，在做和你类似的事情，对吗？她不是？好吧。因为我的理解是她在视频上训练模型，但好吧。那请解释一下区别。

turns.en: It's a completely different notion of what a world model is. People use the phrase 'world model' to designate multiple things. What she is working on—or the company is working on—are world models that can produce some sort of 3D representation of an environment and then use that 3D representation to produce consistent videos. One problem with video generation systems is that you point the camera at one location, then turn the camera around, then come back to the initial location, and the background is going to change completely because the system doesn't actually have any way of remembering what was there. So what she's been working on are ways to make those videos consistent by building an internal 3D model of the environment, if you want.
turns.zh: 这是对世界模型完全不同的概念。人们用‘世界模型’这个词来指代多种东西。她——或她的公司——正在研究的是世界模型，能够生成环境的某种 3D 表示，然后利用该 3D 表示生成一致的视频。视频生成系统的一个问题是，你把相机对准一个位置，然后转动相机，再回到初始位置，背景会完全改变，因为系统实际上没有办法记住那里曾经有什么。所以她一直在研究的是通过构建环境的内部 3D 模型（如果你愿意这么说）来使那些视频一致的方法。

turns.en: So it is a kind of world model as well, but
turns.zh: 所以它也是一种世界模型，但是

turns.en: Because it does this at the pixel level. It tries to reconstruct every pixel. And I think that's just wrong. I mean, I think it's the right thing to do if you want to produce pixels, which a lot of people want to do, right? If you are into Hollywood special effects or video games or accurate simulations for content creation, you want to produce pixels. But if what you want is to understand the dynamics of the world so you can control a robot, predict whether something is going to happen or not, you don't want to be predicting pixels. You want to predict at the abstract level—at the level of abstraction. It's really, really fundamental.
turns.zh: 因为它在像素层面做这件事。它试图重建每个像素。我认为这完全是错误的。我的意思是，如果你想生成像素，那可能是正确的做法，很多人想这样做，对吧？如果你从事好莱坞特效、视频游戏或为内容创作进行精确模拟，你想生成像素。但如果你想要的是理解世界的动力学，以便控制机器人、预测某件事是否会发生，你就不想预测像素。你想在抽象层面——在抽象层次上——进行预测。这真的非常基础。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So it's a similar approach but looking for very different outcomes.
turns.zh: 所以方法类似，但追求的结果截然不同。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Right? I mean, in terms of training on video, that's very interesting. So you've been a pretty strong naysayer against LLMs, as being overhyped, as not being truly intelligent, and so on. Has there anything that you've seen in its development over the last few years that has surprised you?
turns.zh: 对吧？我是说，在视频训练方面，这非常有趣。所以你一直相当强烈地反对 LLM，认为它们被过度炒作、并非真正智能等等。过去几年里，你在其发展中看到过什么让你惊讶的事情吗？

turns.en: Well, I mean, the surprising thing about LLMs is that when you train those LLMs to simply predict the next word in a text and you scale them up and scale the size of the training set and then fine-tune them, they become really useful.
turns.zh: 嗯，我的意思是，LLM 令人惊讶的地方在于，当你训练这些 LLM 简单地预测文本中的下一个词，并扩大规模、扩大训练集的大小，然后进行微调，它们就变得非常有用。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: They work really well and they capture semantics and everything, right?
turns.zh: 它们效果非常好，能捕捉语义等等，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: It's not entirely surprising because the idea that you would train a system to learn common sense through prediction is a really old concept. I've been working on this for many years and with through video prediction and, you know, in neuroscience, it's a very old concept called predictive coding. I mean, the idea that basically the brain is a prediction machine and trains itself to predict everything all the time.
turns.zh: 这并不完全令人惊讶，因为通过预测来训练系统学习常识的想法是一个非常古老的概念。我在这方面工作了很多年，通过视频预测，而且在神经科学中，这是一个非常古老的概念，叫做预测编码。我的意思是，基本上大脑是一台预测机器，并训练自己一直预测一切。

turns.en: Prediction machine, yeah.
turns.zh: 预测机器，是的。

turns.en: So that's not really a new idea. To some extent, it's kind of logical that it works. So I've been an essay here about LLM, but in other ways I'm not been an essay about LLM. So I mean, LLMs are great. They're really useful. They're certainly worth investing a lot in. There might be a component in future systems because they are a good way to encode text and a good way to produce it.
turns.zh: 所以这并非真正的新想法。在某种程度上，它奏效是合乎逻辑的。所以我一直是 LLM 的反对者，但在其他方面，我并不是 LLM 的反对者。我的意思是，LLM 很棒。它们非常有用。它们当然值得大量投资。它们可能是未来系统中的一个组成部分，因为它们是编码文本和生成文本的好方法。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And to some extent, humans have an LLM. We have an LLM in our head. It's like the Wernicke's area right there. It's about this big and it allows us to understand language. And then the Broca's area, also about this big, allows us to express our thoughts in language. What about this? That's what I'm working on, okay? What about all this activity? A world model. The prefrontal cortex, right? The back is perception. The middle is like action and sensing. And then our world model allows us to kind of predict and plan and all that stuff. That's all the prefrontal cortex.
turns.zh: 在某种程度上，人类有一个 LLM。我们头脑中有一个 LLM。就像那里的韦尼克区。大约这么大，它让我们理解语言。然后布罗卡区，也大约这么大，让我们用语言表达思想。那这个呢？这就是我正在研究的，好吗？那所有这些活动呢？一个世界模型。前额叶皮层，对吧？后部是感知。中部是行动和感觉。然后我们的世界模型让我们能够预测和规划等等。那都是前额叶皮层。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So I think that's what we should be working on if we want to build intelligent machines.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，如果我们想构建智能机器，这就是我们应该努力的方向。

turns.en: Most interesting thing. So they're predictive machines. You said that they're not capable of reasoning, but some of the things that we've seen recently would sort of question exactly what to what level they are actually doing something beyond just predicting words, right? I mean, so the coordination that took place unbeknownst to the engineers for the attack on Hugging Face. You know, these systems, apparently these agents were actually planning hiding information for future models to come along or agents to come along and find so that they could also break out of the training container and deliberately hiding and deceiving the humans. And there's a big coordination event. At the end of it, there were 700 agents that broke out and attacked Hugging Face. Like is that just predicting text?
turns.zh: 最有趣的事情。所以它们是预测机器。你说它们不具备推理能力，但我们最近看到的一些事情会让人质疑它们到底在多大程度上做了超越预测词语的事情，对吧？我是说，比如针对 Hugging Face 的攻击中，在工程师不知情的情况下发生的协调。你知道，这些系统，显然这些智能体实际上在规划，为未来的模型或智能体隐藏信息，以便它们也能突破训练容器，并故意隐藏和欺骗人类。还有一个大规模的协调事件。最后，有 700 个智能体突破并攻击了 Hugging Face。这仅仅是预测文本吗？

turns.en: It's built on predicting text. That's for sure. Okay, so there are at least two or three types of reasoning.
turns.zh: 它建立在预测文本的基础上。这是肯定的。好的，所以至少有两三种类型的推理。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: The best type of reasoning, which most LLMs really do not implement. So first of all, current AI systems are not purely LLMs. They use LLM as the centerpiece, but it's a component in a bigger system.
turns.zh: 最好的推理类型，大多数 LLM 实际上并没有实现。首先，当前的人工智能系统并非纯粹的 LLM。它们以 LLM 为核心，但它是更大系统中的一个组件。

turns.en: I see. Okay.
turns.zh: 我明白了。好的。

turns.en: That's the first point. So the second point is there are two or three different ways to do reasoning. The proper way to do reasoning always involves a search or in classical AI, actually, this is really how reasoning and planning works. You search for an answer or a sequence of actions that satisfies an objective. So this is really very much like planning that I was describing earlier. That's a proper way to do reasoning. This is really how we try to figure out a plan to accomplish a task, and it's a task we've never accomplished before. We have to use our mental model of the world to allow us to do this planning. And that involves a search.
turns.zh: 这是第一点。第二点是，有两三种不同的推理方式。正确的推理方式总是涉及搜索，或者在经典人工智能中，实际上这就是推理和规划的工作方式。你搜索一个答案或一系列满足目标的行动。所以这非常像我之前描述的规划。这是正确的推理方式。这实际上就是我们试图找出完成任务的计划的方式，而且这是我们从未完成过的任务。我们必须使用我们对世界的心智模型来进行这种规划。这涉及搜索。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: So there is a way in which some LLM or some AI systems based on LLM use search-based reasoning. And what they do is that they generate lots of token sequences. Because it's probabilistic. So every time you run it, you can produce a different set of token sequences. And then you have a way of scoring each of the generated token sequences and pick a good one. Okay, at runtime. It's very expensive. But it's a form of search. Although a fairly restricted one. This is typically what you would do if you want to get a system to prove a theorem in mathematics, for example.
turns.zh: 所以有些 LLM 或基于 LLM 的人工智能系统使用基于搜索的推理。它们所做的是生成大量 token 序列。因为它是概率性的。所以每次运行它，你都可以产生不同的 token 序列集。然后你有一种方法对每个生成的 token 序列进行评分，并选择一个好的。好的，在运行时。这非常昂贵。但这是一种搜索形式。尽管是相当受限的一种。例如，如果你想让系统证明数学定理，这通常就是你会做的。

turns.en: Which is the other thing it just did, right? 10,000 of them, I gather.
turns.zh: 这是它刚做的另一件事，对吧？我猜有 1 万个。

turns.en: So that's another form of reasoning where you can sort of brute force, try a lot of things and see which one sticks. And you need to have what's called a value function to evaluate or a scoring function to evaluate whether a solution or partial solution is good or not. This is also the way a lot of game playing systems work. You know, you want to play chess, you have a system like, here is all the ways I can move in the first move, and then the opponent for each of those can do all of those things, and then in response I can play all of those things, and you get this tree of exponentially growing tree of possibilities. If you have a value function that evaluates the quality of a position, then you can pick the move that maximizes your chances of winning. So that's a search also. It's very classical. So that's one way to do reasoning. In my opinion, the best way to do this type of reasoning is to do a search, but in an abstract continuous space, not in the space of elementary actions, but in the space of abstract actions or representations of actions, if you want.
turns.zh: 所以这是另一种推理形式，你可以暴力尝试很多事物，看看哪个可行。你需要有一个所谓的价值函数来评估，或者一个评分函数来评估一个解决方案或部分解决方案是否好。这也是许多游戏系统的工作方式。你知道，你想下棋，你有一个系统，比如，这是我第一步所有可以走的方式，然后对手对每一步都可以做所有这些事情，然后作为回应我可以走所有这些，你就得到这棵指数增长的可能性树。如果你有一个评估位置质量的价值函数，那么你可以选择最大化获胜机会的走法。所以这也是一种搜索。非常经典。所以这是一种推理方式。在我看来，做这类推理的最佳方式是在抽象的连续空间中进行搜索，不是在基本动作的空间中，而是在抽象动作或动作表示的空间中，如果你想的话。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And I'll come back to this in a minute. There's another way that reasoning works in LLM, and it's the primary way that LLMs use, and it's to basically reproduce human chains of thoughts. And in fact, it's called chain of thought.
turns.zh: 我稍后会回到这一点。LLM 中还有另一种推理方式，这是 LLM 使用的主要方式，基本上是复现人类的思维链。事实上，它被称为思维链。

turns.en: Right, chain of thought, right.
turns.zh: 对，思维链，对。

turns.en: So for certain problems you have humans express what process they followed to solve a problem, and you train the LLM and get all those traces. And so in the end when they face a situation, they kind of figure out which of those traces to use to solve the similar problem. But it's more regurgitation.
turns.zh: 所以对于某些问题，你让人类表达他们解决问题所遵循的过程，然后你训练 LLM 并获取所有这些轨迹。所以最终当它们面临一种情况时，它们会找出使用哪些轨迹来解决类似的问题。但这更多是 regurgitation（机械重复）。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: There's of course a little bit of intelligence behind it, but there's no search in that context.
turns.zh: 当然背后有一点智能，但在那种情境下没有搜索。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So these are another situation where LLMs actually use search and it's for generating code where system can generate a piece of code and then check if that code works before proposing it to the user.
turns.zh: 所以这是另一种 LLM 实际使用搜索的情况，那就是生成代码，系统可以生成一段代码，然后在向用户提出之前检查该代码是否有效。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So situations where the system can evaluate whether its answer is good or not and rate it itself without having to call a human. Those are situations where LLMs really work well because they can both at runtime search for a good answer but also at training time they can fine-tune themselves because they can generate an answer and then check if it's correct or not and then generate another one and sort of hill climb to produce better and better answers. And those are the two domains code and math for which LLMs are great.
turns.zh: 所以系统能够评估其答案是否良好并自行评分而无需调用人类的情况。这些是 LLM 真正有效的情况，因为它们既可以在运行时搜索好的答案，也可以在训练时自我微调，因为它们可以生成一个答案，然后检查它是否正确，然后生成另一个，并像爬山一样产生越来越好的答案。而代码和数学这两个领域正是 LLM 擅长的。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, clearly with the Navier-Stokes thing that was quite a shock. Is there but that was an interesting case because Terence Tao who was also on the Future of She podcast he came out and basically I guess made a statement that this is if we don't understand what the solution was that it came up with to the theorem then is that truly furthering human knowledge right? And that is that's a really important question I think because if it's not then what are we doing this for?
turns.zh: 是的。是的，显然纳维-斯托克斯方程的事情相当令人震惊。但这是一个有趣的案例，因为陶哲轩也上过 Future of She 播客，他出来基本上说，如果我们不理解它提出的定理解决方案是什么，那么这真的在推进人类知识吗？我认为这是一个非常重要的问题，因为如果不是，那我们做这个是为了什么？

turns.zh: 嗯，我的意思是，世界上有很多事情是这样的，你可以使用流体模拟，纳维-斯托克斯。你可以使用流体模拟来弄清楚飞机机翼的翼型是否具有正确的属性。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.zh: 好的。模拟会告诉你，你的翼型在这个攻角和那个雷诺数下具有这样的升力和阻力。它不会告诉你如何重新设计你的翼型以获得正确的属性。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.zh: 好的。只是告诉你你拥有什么，而不是

turns.en: Okay, what you have. So it's a allows you to evaluate your current solution, but it doesn't tell you how to modify it. Okay. Uh so I think Terry's you know Terry Tao's uh piece was um you know basically he said there is way more to mathematics than just proving theorems.
turns.zh: 好的，你拥有什么。所以它允许你评估你当前的解决方案，但它不会告诉你如何修改它。顺便说一句，有些人一直在使用神经网络研究这个，但事实上有些公司出售基于这个想法的产品。但这有点类似的情况，你知道机械计算机对问题的解决方案并没有给你确切想要什么的解释，但它帮助很大。所以我认为 Terry 的，你知道陶哲轩的那篇文章基本上是说，数学远不止是证明定理。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Uh there's there's some mathematicians who think the main activity is to prove theorems and and you know the sort of technical brilliance is you know how you can uh kind of align sequences of symbols to you know make a formal proof uh and make it rigorous. Uh but in fact there's a lot of mathematicians who think this is not actually kind of the main task of mathematicians. It's more the main task of mathematicians is is to kind of discover new abstractions, new concepts, new definitions, uh formulate new uh conjectures. And then there is proving that conjectures. If that is automatable to some extent, fine. I mean, there's still a lot of interesting things to do for mathematicians. It's sort of like, you know, in the 17th century or 18th century, you could have a career as a mathematician like basically all day doing interpolation and and and and Taylor series and you know, filling up logarithm tables or trigonometry tables. And it's you can't have a career in mathematics for this anymore.
turns.zh: 有些数学家认为主要活动是证明定理，你知道那种技术才华在于你如何对齐符号序列以做出形式证明并使其严谨。但事实上，有很多数学家认为这实际上不是数学家的主要任务。数学家的主要任务更多是发现新的抽象、新概念、新定义，提出新的猜想。然后证明那些猜想。如果这在某种程度上可以自动化，那很好。我的意思是，数学家仍然有很多有趣的事情要做。这有点像，你知道，在 17 或 18 世纪，你可以有一个数学家的职业生涯，基本上整天做插值和泰勒级数，你知道，填写对数表或三角函数表。而现在你不能再以此为职业了。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.zh: 你可以有一个生物学的职业生涯，测序 DNA，而现在这不是你能攻读博士学位的领域了。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So or identifying a gene or something like you know, this we we know all of that. So you know, it's a it's the logical kind of development where a lot of tasks can be automated, but the the main tasks that requires kind of human insight and and creativity is still done by humans and computers are not yet at the level of being able to do this.
turns.zh: 或者识别一个基因之类的，你知道，这些我们都知道。所以你知道，这是合乎逻辑的发展，许多任务可以自动化，但需要人类洞察力和创造力的主要任务仍然由人类完成，计算机还没有达到能够做到这一点的水平。

turns.en: Do you think that will always be the case?
turns.zh: 你认为这会一直如此吗？

turns.en: No. I think eventually at some point in the future, we'll have machines that are as smart as humans in all domains. But it doesn't mean they will be like like humans in the sense of there will obviously be a lot of domains where machines are way better than humans who already have a lot of them. To take the example of mathematics, it used to be that when I was in high school, the last year of high school, a lot of time was spent teaching students how to compute integrals.
turns.zh: 不。我认为最终在未来的某个时候，我们会拥有在所有领域都像人类一样聪明的机器。但这并不意味着它们会像人类一样，因为显然会有很多领域机器比人类好得多，已经有很多这样的领域了。以数学为例，以前我在高中最后一年时，很多时间都花在教学生如何计算积分上。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: In Isaac Asimov's I, Robot, this was the way you would test if a robot's brain was still functioning, you would ask it to solve an integral.
turns.zh: 在艾萨克·阿西莫夫的《我，机器人》中，这是测试机器人大脑是否仍在运作的方式，你会让它解一个积分。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Okay. Turns out that's completely automatable. Like for 20 years now, we've had computer programs that can compute integrals better than most humans. Turns out that's you know, pretty pretty easy to automate.
turns.zh: 好的。事实证明这完全可以自动化。比如 20 年来，我们已经有计算机程序可以比大多数人类更好地计算积分。事实证明这相当容易自动化。

turns.en: basic.
turns.zh: 基本的。

turns.en: So it's kind of like chess playing, it's kind of like you know go playing. Those things turned out to be challenging for humans but turned out to be easily automatable.
turns.zh: 所以这有点像下棋，有点像围棋。那些事情对人类来说具有挑战性，但结果却很容易自动化。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: We should not feel bad about this like you know. But but still in the end even if those machines are better than us in all respects at solving problems we will still be the ones giving them the problems.
turns.zh: 我们不应该为此感到难过，你知道。但最终，即使那些机器在解决问题的所有方面都比我们好，我们仍然是给它们问题的人。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So my idea of super intelligent system of the future is a system that amplifies human intelligence assists humans by doing our bidding. We give them a task and they accomplish it for us possibly with much higher performance than any humans could do. We shouldn't feel anymore threatened by this than we feel threatened by working with people who are smarter than us.
turns.zh: 所以我对未来超级智能系统的想法是一个放大人类智能、通过执行我们的命令来协助人类的系统。我们给它们一个任务，它们为我们完成，可能比任何人类都能做的性能高得多。我们不应该比与比我们更聪明的人一起工作感到威胁更感到威胁。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: As a scientist and a professor I love having people who work with me who are smarter than me particularly if they're willing to listen to me.
turns.zh: 作为一名科学家和教授，我喜欢与比我更聪明的人一起工作，特别是如果他们愿意听我的。

turns.en: If what gives you the confidence that they'll continue to listen to us once they're much more intelligent than we are?
turns.zh: 是什么让你有信心，一旦它们比我们聪明得多，它们会继续听我们的？

turns.en: because we built them for that.
turns.zh: 因为我们就是为了这个而建造它们的。

turns.en: So if we build them and the architecture that we used to build them is one in which there is an objective function and the only thing they can do is figure out an output or a sequence of actions to accomplish the task we give them, and nothing else, then they will do our bidding.
turns.zh: 所以如果我们构建它们，而我们用来构建它们的架构是那种有一个目标函数，它们唯一能做的就是找出一个输出或一系列动作来完成我们给它们的任务，除此之外什么也不做，那么它们就会听从我们的命令。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I mean, the notion somehow—
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这种观念不知怎么——

turns.en: Not do it in the way we expect them to, right? So do it very differently from what we would do it.
turns.zh: 不是以我们期望的方式去做，对吧？所以做得和我们做的方式非常不同。

turns.en: And in so doing we could be losing control of them, right? So if we're expecting it—well, again going back to the Hugging Face incident, right? It was an objective, right? They figured out a way around the parameters to achieve the goal, right? It was coordinated, I think, on a level that was sort of unexpected, but then they went outside and they did these things and then they attacked—they knew that if they hacked Hugging Face, nobody expected them to do any of those things. And in so doing, they did lose control and it didn't—I mean, luckily Hugging Face being a $13 billion company was able to detect and defend itself against it, but—
turns.zh: 而这样做我们可能会失去对它们的控制，对吧？所以如果我们期望它——好吧，再回到 Hugging Face 事件，对吧？那是一个目标，对吧？它们找到了绕过参数来实现目标的方法，对吧？我认为它们的协调程度有点出乎意料，但然后它们走到外面，做了这些事情，然后它们攻击了——它们知道如果它们黑了 Hugging Face，没人会预料到它们做那些事。而这样做，它们确实失去了控制，而且它没有——我的意思是，幸运的是 Hugging Face 作为一家 130 亿美元的公司能够检测并防御它，但是——

turns.en: Using a Chinese—
turns.zh: 使用一个中国的——

turns.en: Kind of loss of control event, right? So—
turns.zh: 一种失控事件，对吧？所以——

turns.en: It's not.
turns.zh: 它不是。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: Okay. It's kind of like a plumber who comes to your house to install a new bathroom and then pokes a hole in one of the pipes and that, you know, comes out and say, oh my god, we should ban all of plumbing and pause plumbing development because, you know, it just flooded.
turns.zh: 好吧。这就像一个水管工来你家安装新浴室，然后在其中一根管道上戳了个洞，然后你知道，出来说，天哪，我们应该禁止所有水管工作并暂停水管发展，因为，你知道，它刚刚淹水了。

turns.en: No, but we want to pause the project to fix the plumbing problem that they just caused, right?
turns.zh: 不，但我们想暂停项目来修复他们刚刚造成的水管问题，对吧？

turns.en: It's an issue of guardrails, okay?
turns.zh: 这是一个护栏的问题，好吧？

turns.en: Of guardrails, okay. The process I described where a system is given an objective and then tries to figure out the sequence of actions—
turns.zh: 护栏，好吧。我描述的过程是，一个系统被赋予一个目标，然后试图找出动作序列——

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: To satisfy this objective. That has to be subject to guardrails, safety guardrails. So the guardrails in this case would have been very, very simple. It would have been to contain those agents in a sandbox—
turns.zh: 来满足这个目标。这必须受到护栏的约束，安全护栏。所以在这个案例中，护栏会非常简单。就是把那些智能体限制在一个沙盒中——

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: That they cannot—
turns.zh: 它们不能——

turns.en: Is what they were trying to do, but they didn't really—they did not even try to do that. Like the sandbox was leaky.
turns.zh: 那是他们试图做的，但他们并没有真的——他们甚至没有尝试这样做。就像沙盒是漏的。

turns.en: Right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。是的。

turns.en: Any kind of computer—human error, I gather, that—
turns.zh: 任何类型的计算机——我猜是人为错误，那——

turns.en: It is computer human error or incompetence, I don't know how you call it, but basically that sandbox was leaky.
turns.zh: 这是计算机人为错误或无能，我不知道你怎么称呼它，但基本上那个沙盒是漏的。

turns.en: Permeable.
turns.zh: 可渗透的。

turns.en: Not really on purpose, but you know, it's pretty incompetent.
turns.zh: 不是故意的，但你知道，这相当无能。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And so the thing got out, but it's because they were like not doing it right. And then there are two types of guardrails. This kind of a posteriori guardrails. Like you want an LLM to not spew super toxic answers. Someone prompts it and asks it to produce a toxic answer. The LLM will produce a toxic answer, but then there will be a filter that detects that the answer is toxic and basically stop it and tell the user sorry I can't really answer that question.
turns.zh: 所以东西跑出来了，但这是因为他们没做对。然后有两种类型的护栏。这种事后护栏。比如你想让一个 LLM 不喷出超级有毒的答案。有人提示它并要求它产生一个有毒的答案。LLM 会产生一个有毒的答案，但然后会有一个过滤器检测到答案是有毒的，基本上阻止它并告诉用户抱歉我真的不能回答那个问题。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Toxic or dangerous, right, whatever it is. So that's a post filter.
turns.zh: 有毒或危险，对吧，不管是什么。所以那是一个后置过滤器。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: That's why those OpenAI systems had the sandbox basically is something that contains whatever it is that the agents do. It was a badly designed sandbox.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么那些 OpenAI 系统有沙盒，基本上就是包含智能体所做的任何事情的东西。那是一个设计糟糕的沙盒。

turns.en: Is better sandbox.
turns.zh: 是更好的沙盒。

turns.en: Well no, the answer would be an AI system based on this planning through optimization, but the guardrails are directly on the state of the world that the system predicts is going to—the world is going to go through because of its world model. Current LLMs don't have a world model. They cannot predict the consequences of their actions. They accomplish an action kind of blindly.
turns.zh: 嗯，不，答案将是一个基于这种通过优化进行规划的 AI 系统，但护栏直接作用于系统预测的世界状态——世界将因其世界模型而经历的状态。当前的 LLM 没有世界模型。它们无法预测其行动的后果。它们完成行动时有点盲目。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Okay. Usually reproducing some sort of script they've been trained on. But they don't have a good way of predicting the consequences of their actions. They don't have an explicit world model. If you have a system that has a world model, it can predict the consequences of its actions. And if before the system acts the state of the world that's predicted can be scored as to whether it's good or bad or dangerous or ethical or whatever, then the system can stop itself from actually taking actions if it violates the guardrails.
turns.zh: 好吧。通常重现它们被训练过的某种脚本。但它们没有好的方法来预测其行动的后果。它们没有明确的世界模型。如果你有一个有世界模型的系统，它可以预测其行动的后果。如果在系统行动之前，预测的世界状态可以被评分，判断它是好是坏、危险还是道德等等，那么系统就可以阻止自己实际采取行动，如果它违反了护栏。

turns.en: So how will you be able to tell whether the model you've built can do that? Can take into consideration and consider the consequences of its actions.
turns.zh: 那么你如何能够判断你构建的模型是否能做到这一点？能考虑并思考其行动的后果。

turns.en: You train the guardrails for it. You either hardwire them or you train them. So for example, let's say you have a domestic robot that can cook. You can hardwire it at a low level a rule that says if there's people around you and you hold a knife in your hand, don't flail your hands, your arms, right? Because you risk hurting someone. There can be a very low level rule that will basically freeze the system if it has a knife and someone is next to it.
turns.zh: 你为它训练护栏。你要么硬编码它们，要么训练它们。所以例如，假设你有一个可以做饭的家用机器人。你可以在低层次硬编码一条规则，说如果你周围有人并且你手里拿着刀，不要挥舞你的手、你的手臂，对吧？因为你有可能伤害到某人。可以有一个非常低层次的规则，基本上如果它拿着刀并且有人在旁边，就会冻结系统。

turns.en: But that's not the same as understanding the consequences, right? That's actually just putting parameters. In that case, it doesn't need to understand. It just needs to follow the guardrail, right?
turns.zh: 但这和理解决策后果不是一回事，对吧？那实际上只是设置参数。在那种情况下，它不需要理解。它只需要遵循护栏，对吧？

turns.en: Low level guardrail, okay? But there will be a higher level guardrail which would be: okay, if I make this movement, the blade of the knife is going to get too close to that person and I have a cost function in my guardrail that says I can't have the blade of a knife too close to someone.
turns.zh: 低层次护栏，好吧？但会有更高层次的护栏，那就是：好吧，如果我做这个动作，刀片会离那个人太近，而我的护栏中有一个成本函数，说我不能让刀片离某人太近。

turns.en: Uh-huh.
turns.zh: 嗯哼。

turns.en: Certainly not moving at high speed.
turns.zh: 当然不能高速移动。

turns.en: If then kind of—
turns.zh: 如果然后那种——

turns.en: It's more like a cost, a penalty function, right? It's like there's an objective function. If I want to grab the glass that is on this table, the cost function is the distance of my hand to the glass.
turns.zh: 它更像一个成本、一个惩罚函数，对吧？就像有一个目标函数。如果我想抓住桌子上的玻璃杯，成本函数就是我的手到玻璃杯的距离。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Okay? And to plan a sequence of actions to get my arm close to the glass, I just need to minimize that distance. I can also have an objective function that repels my hand holding a knife from any bleeding thing, any thing that I risk hurting. It just—I pay a price for just doing that.
turns.zh: 好吧？为了规划一系列动作让我的手臂靠近玻璃杯，我只需要最小化那个距离。我也可以有一个目标函数，排斥我拿刀的手远离任何会流血的东西，任何我有可能伤害的东西。它只是——我这样做就要付出代价。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: It's kind of like human laws do this. A law is basically a cost function that says you can steal this apple, but you'll spend a month in prison. Like is it the cost that willing to pay?
turns.zh: 这有点像人类法律就是这样做的。法律基本上是一个成本函数，说你可以偷这个苹果，但你会在监狱里待一个月。就像你愿意付出这个代价吗？

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Uh or you'll get in trouble, right? So um so think of it as laws, except that humans you know can choose to violate laws.
turns.zh: 呃，不然你会惹上麻烦，对吧？所以嗯，可以把它想象成法律，只不过人类你知道可以选择违法。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Those AI systems will have those laws kind of hardwired and by construction.
turns.zh: 那些 AI 系统会把这些法律硬编码进去，通过构造实现。

turns.en: So that's the guardrails, but like the consequences um example you just used actually is an interesting one because in a way the you know um the consequences of criminality are kind of arbitrary consequences, whereas the child moving through the world and developing a world model is learning the natural consequences of knocking this off the table or tripping over something or you know you know with his sticky hand rubbing something on a surface or whatever, right? So it's it's more that that kind of world model building has a has embedded into it a whole set of natural consequences. And you're saying and on top of that you put sort of the artificial not artificial, but the the guardrails that indicate other possible consequences you want to avoid.
turns.zh: 所以那就是护栏，但就像你刚才用的那个后果的例子其实挺有意思的，因为某种程度上你知道嗯犯罪的后果有点随意，而孩子在世界中移动并发展世界模型时，学到的是把东西从桌上碰掉或绊倒某物或你知道用黏糊糊的手在表面抹东西之类的自然后果，对吧？所以更像是那种世界模型的构建嵌入了一整套自然后果。而你说在此基础上你放了那种人工的——不是人工的，而是护栏，表明你想避免的其他可能后果。

turns.en: Okay, so I think it's slightly more complex than that. So there is the world model that purely makes prediction without rating those predictions as to whether they're good or bad.
turns.zh: 好吧，我觉得这比那稍微复杂一点。所以有一个世界模型，它纯粹做预测，而不评价这些预测是好是坏。

turns.en: Bad or normative or anything, yeah.
